Can Language Models Play the Wikipedia Game?
Alexander Hickey, Joanna Knight, and James Bishop
The Alan Turing Institute, 96 Euston Rd., London NW1 2DB, UK
ahickey@turing.ac.uk
Abstract
Language models increasingly support or automate information retrieval from
document collections too large to index.
This task is difficult when it requires
specialist linguistic or scientific knowledge. We used the Wikipedia Game to test

language models on an analogous information retrieval task. In the game, play-
ers must reach a target article using only article links.
We compared sentence
embedding models and LLMs across five Wikipedia languages and five academic-
literature datasets. We construct very large local graphs of Wikipedia pages and
of paper citations using OpenAlex and provide code to build and navigate them.
This allows the study of language models’ navigation capabilities without relying on

third-party APIs. We compared the models with human and TF-IDF benchmarks.
The Wikipedia Game format enables robust comparisons across techniques, lan-
guages, and domains. No model significantly outperformed humans, although the
best models (GPT-o3 mini, GPT-4o, QwQ:32B, and DeepSeek-R1:70B) achieved
comparable success. Performance and rankings varied across languages and topics,
with implications for practitioners utilising these techniques.

Introduction
This project investigates the capabilities and limitations of language models when au-
tomatically navigating the content of unstructured document stores. Language models
are often used to automate time-consuming tasks, and many of these, such as informa-
tion retrieval, text classification, and question answering, require the models to connect
concepts semantically [1, 7, 19, 20, 41].

Wikipedia is a free online encyclopedia that contains millions of hyperlinked articles

created by over a quarter of a million editors and is available in over 300 languages.
In the Wikipedia Game, participants start with two random articles and are expected
to navigate between them by clicking only on links within each article. Succeeding in
the Wikipedia Game requires players to continuously evaluate the relatedness between
the target article and the linked articles available. While sentence embedding models

Previous literature has discussed the Wikipedia Game, and recent natural language

building these graphs to facilitate utilising these datasets, we can see how varieties of

to real-world applications [6].
These findings can help inform individuals looking to

1.1
Wikipedia as a Graph
English Wikipedia has over six million articles, which contain nearly 300 million links
between them, making it the largest reference work in history. This encyclopedia can

be conceptualised as a graph comprising connected nodes (the articles) and edges (the
hyperlinks between the articles) [8]. Doing so has enabled other researchers to construct
a knowledge graph [46] or identify useful missing links [40]. As Wikipedia is both human-
written text and organised within a structured format, it has been harnessed for topic
classification [17], improving the performance of foundation models [52], and providing

reliable ground truth data for named entity recognition [3].
1.2
Wikipedia as a Testing Ground
This work leverages the size and structure of Wikipedia and similar datasets to provide
a robust challenge for language models to utilise the semantic information they con-
tain. Previous research has capitalised on these properties of Wikipedia to assess word
embeddings and graph search algorithms and construct benchmarks [4, 10, 14]. Other

studies have leveraged human performance in the Wikipedia game as a source of seman-
tic information [48,50]. This work builds on these previous studies by assessing sentence
embeddings and LLMs, making it possible to compare NLP methods and human abilities.
Beyond language models, Wikipedia is an excellent training dataset for graph neural
networks [28,39]. Additionally, these same techniques can be applied to citation networks

in academic literature to more accurately assign papers to an academic topic [24].
1.3
Generative and Embedding Models
One may naively consider the Wikipedia Game to be a sequence of judging how re-
lated each potential next article is to the target article. Sentence embedding models are

particularly well-suited for this task [5] as these models aim to produce a vector that
numerically represents the meaning conveyed by a given sentence [37]. Embedding mod-
els can be optimised to connect related concepts or to focus on distinguishing topics or
sentiments [2], work in multiple languages [38] and address specialised domains [35].
When people play the Wikipedia Game, they do not just jump incrementally to the

most related article but are instead planning a route ahead. This kind of planning and
strategy cannot be reproduced by an embedding model that relies solely on a greedy
iterative approach that always seeks the next ‘closest’ article. Reinforcement Learning
(RL) can be used to incorporate strategic considerations into deep learning techniques,
and there are numerous examples of combining RL with NLP techniques (e.g. playing
text adventure games [31,34]).

There is some evidence that LLMs can plan and show strategic considerations [15,53],
which could give an advantage over embedding models. However, there are many exam-
ples where their strategic considerations fall short of what might be expected based on
their language comprehension ability [32,44]. This issue may arise because the majority
of LLM training is based on next-word prediction; it is theorised that the model’s rea-

soning processes quickly deteriorate once it is outside examples provided in the training
data [29,51]. Comparing LLMs’ performance at this task to sentence embedding models,
which can only provide semantic comparisons of sentences, might help illuminate their
strategic ability.

2.2
OpenAlex
OpenAlex is a dataset of metadata (including the title, authors, abstract, and references)

about academic works. The OpenAlex data have been used to create graphs with the
references and citations as the links between the articles, and the abstracts were used like
the summaries. To create datasets more similar to Wikipedia, this project limited the
type of work to ‘articles’ (other types of work that were excluded include ‘book chapters’,
‘dissertations’ and ‘letters’). Unlike the Wikipedia dataset, the OpenAlex datasets are

symmetric graphs because if Article A references Article B, then Article B will be cited
by Article A.
The OpenAlex dataset was categorised based on each paper’s primary academic field
to create multiple graphs (additional details in Appendix B). Using the primary topic
categorisation, five subjects were chosen (see Figure 1A). The connectivity of the graphs
reflects the referencing patterns within each academic field, leading to significant varia-

3
Experimental Setup
For each of the datasets listed in Figure 1A, a set of 10,000 pairs of articles were randomly
generated, with each pair representing one ‘game’. One article in each pair was labelled

the source article and the other the target article; the pair was discarded if it was not
possible to navigate between them.
The goal of the game is to navigate to the target article using only the links in the
graph. In the two formulations of the game, the agent player may only see the title of each
link or the title and the summary text of each possible link (resembling the mouse-over
preview in Wikipedia). In both formulations, the agent is allowed to see the summary of

the target article. Only the choices on the ‘current’ article can be viewed before one is
selected: the agent is not allowed to look further ahead or to work backwards from the
target article.
The same set of games was used for each agent, but resource constraints meant that
not all agents could play all 10,000 games. For the experiments using OpenAlex, the
target articles were filtered on the language field of ‘English’; however, the relaxation of
this constraint is explored in Appendix O.

When the agents played the game, there were a few ways that it could end, the
simplest being that the target article was reached successfully. However, the agent can
fail to reach the target article in multiple ways, the most common being not reaching the
target within 100 steps. It was also possible for the model to reach a dead end, for the
LLM-based agents to repeatedly generate an article title that does not exist or reject the

request, and for reasoning models to fail to provide an answer. More details on this are
in Appendix L.
4
Agents
This work considers two types of language models: sentence embedding models and
LLMs. We compare their ability to play the Wikipedia Game to a statistical approach
and human attempts. The setup for all these methods is optimised to compare how these
techniques might be used in a real-world setting.
4.1
Sentence Embeddings

4.1
Sentence Embeddings
Sentence embedding models map text to numerical vectors within a high-dimensional
space where semantically similar sentences are positioned closely together [18]. We de-
signed an agent that used a pre-trained sentence embedding model to select the link at
each stage of the game with the ‘closest’ summary sentence or title to the target summary
sentence. The ‘closest’ link was determined by the minimum cosine distance. As with all
5

the agents, additional logic prevents them from returning to an article they have already
visited to avoid becoming trapped in loops.
It is possible to play the game either by comparing the summaries or the titles of the
available articles. Both of these versions of the game were considered, and the results
here focus on using the summary embeddings. The impact on performance when only
using the titles can be found in Appendix K.

using the titles can be found in Appendix K.
To aid readability, we will focus on the performance of five of the thirteen embedding
models studied in this work. E5-Small is a multilingual embedding model produced by
Microsoft [45]. AllMPNetBase is recommended by the Sentence Transformers documen-
tation and is a comparable size to E5-Small, but is only trained on English language
data [37]. MiniLM-L6 was one of the smallest models considered with only 22.7 mil-

lion parameters [38, 47]. Roberta makes use of the well-known BERT architecture and
is fine-tuned to produce an embedding model [22, 38]. Glove works by averaging the
individual word embedding, which makes it much faster in inference than similarly sized
models [36,37]. The other models are listed in Appendix E.
4.2
Prompting LLMs
LLMs used here generate human-like text by predicting each word incrementally. By

crafting detailed and specific starting text, known as the prompt, LLMs can be directed to
perform precise tasks such as code synthesis, text labelling, and machine translation [16,
30,43]. Including all the necessary information in the prompt is crucial for maximising
the capabilities of these models.
This work used thirteen different LLMs (listed in Appendix F), including the full
suite of Llama3 models, which range from 1 to 405 billion parameters [11,23]. A Gemma2

model was also used, which has 27 billion parameters [42]. OpenAI’s GPT-4o was the
largest LLM used in this work with its smaller version, GPT-4o mini. However, due to
the cost of running GPT-4o, the number of games played using this agent was limited
to 100 and restricted to only a few datasets. There were also 5 "reasoning (R)" LLMs
evaluated, which included DeepSeek(DS) R1 [12] and Qwen with Questions (QwQ).
Appendix G shows that the larger LLMs are able to explain how to play the Wikipedia

game. The agent prompts an LLM by informing it that it is participating in the Wikipedia
Game, providing a summary of the target article, and asking which article to choose
from a list of titles. This requires a significant amount of information to be provided to
the LLM, which can negatively affect its performance [21]. Two key adjustments were
implemented to address this issue. Firstly, a maximum limit of 500 links for GPT and

200 links for the other models from the current article was established. In preliminary
experiments, GPT-4o was able to cope with a longer prompt and still succeeded, but the
success rate of all LLMs improved when the number of titles was limited. Secondly, the
prompt included only the titles of the linked articles rather than the article summaries.
These adaptions greatly improved the reliability of the prompting method.

As an LLM can, in principle, output any text, a title that does not match any in
the list provided may be generated. In this case, the LLM is prompted again up to four
more times with an extra paragraph emphasising the task. The step counts shown in
6

the results record the number of articles visited, not the number of times the LLM is
queried. For experimental consistency, the same prompt was used for all non-reasoning
LLMs, and the article limit was set high enough to only affect a small minority of articles.
Further details can be found in Appendix H.
4.3
Reasoning LLMs
This work also considered evaluating an LLM in reasoning mode where the LLM can
generate a ‘thinking’ block of text before providing the answer. We evaluated eight of

these LLMs in this way. For GPT-o3 mini, this was done by using the same prompt
as with the GPT-4o model, but allowing reasoning through the API. The open-source
models were given chain-of-thought prompting and could provide an answer (contained
in <answer> tags) in the output text. The DeepSeek (DS) and QwQ models are trained
for this behaviour, while the Llama and Gemma models were not. To distinguish which
setting the models were evaluated in, an (R) is placed after the name of the models

evaluated in the reasoning format. Other than the requested format, the experiment was
the same for the reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs.
4.4
TF-IDF
A non-deep-learning benchmark was created using term frequency-inverse document fre-
quency (TF-IDF) - a statistical approach that assesses the importance of a word to a
document based on its frequency in the corpus. For each dataset, a corpus was created
using a sample of 100,000 articles from that dataset. This does mean that some of the

corpora may be more representative of some datasets than others; for example, 100,000
articles is a greater proportion of the Bengali Wikipedia dataset than the English. The
articles used in the sample are not held separately and may appear in the game. Details
on how the TF-IDF values are calculated can be found in Appendix D.
4.5
Humans
Nine human players attempted a sample of games for the English Wikipedia dataset to

act as a benchmark. These games were not played under strict experimental conditions,
and the players were requested to self-report their success. We used the website Wik-
iSpeedrun3 to provide a timer and count of steps taken. To increase the number of games
played, a time limit of 10 minutes was used instead of a step limit, with players aware of
this limit. In total, 109 games were played, and an overlap of games was avoided between
the players.

Success Rate

5.1
Success Rate
Figure 2A shows the success rate of a selection of the models on the English Wikipedia
graph. A game was considered a success if the model reached the target article from
the start article in 100 steps. Figure 2A shows that GPT-o3 mini (R) had the highest
success rate, comparable to that for humans.
Many sentence embedding models were able to perform similarly to the largest of the
open non-reasoning LLMs, as shown in Figure 2B. The optimum formulation was used

for both model types, so the embedding models used summaries of the linked articles,
whereas the LLMs were only shown the title. Appendix K shows there was a measurable
but not catastrophic drop in the success rate when the embedding models were only
shown the title of the articles.
Unlike the embedding models, the performance of the LLMs severely deteriorated
8

with decreasing model size, which may be related to the model’s ability to stay on task
reliably. This is seen in the much higher tendency for the smaller LLMs to hallucinate.
Reasoning models did manage to provide more accurate answers for the same-sized LLM,
but the smallest reasoning model, DS-R1:8b, did not complete the task. Appendix L
shows the reasons for failure by the different models.
TF-IDF was also effective at the task. The corpus for the TF-IDF model was gen-

erated with a sample from the article summaries used to play the game, and it is likely
that this technique would not be as performant if this construction was not possible.
Appendix M shows the success rate for TF-IDF models on the OpenAlex datasets when
English Wikipedia was used as the corpus, as evidence for this.
5.2
Efficiency
Figure 3 examines the efficiency of the various agents for the games where they succeeded,

as measured by the number of steps taken to reach the target article. Figures 3A, 3B,
and 3C show histograms of the number of extra steps taken above the optimal route
for GPT-4o, DS-R1:70B (R) and E5-Small, which seems to follow a negative binomial
distribution. The figures show that GPT-4o can succeed in fewer steps for a greater
proportion of games than E5-Small. This reflects differences in how the types of models

played the game. An example of the routes taken by E5-Small and GPT-4o on the same
game illustrates this in Appendix N.
Figure 3D shows a clear distinction between human performance and that of GPT
and DS-R1; even though both approaches achieved a comparable success rate, humans
were able to succeed with fewer steps. As the LLM agents allowed five retries in the
event of hallucinations, the LLM models can be considered even less efficient if the

number of queries is counted rather than the number of steps. The LLMs of Llama:405B
and GPT-4o mini can be more efficient than the sentence embedding models. Trained
reasoning models were also comparable in efficiency to the non-reasoning LLMs of similar
performance. This may be indicative of strategies for playing the Wikipedia Game being
taken into account by LLMs over the embedding models. The language models’ step

distributions did not differ measurably from a geometric distribution (i.e. a negative
binomial with n ≈1), but the human games do, even when games more than 10 steps
above optimal are ignored (Appendix J).

7
Discussion
This report shows that sentence embedding models and LLMs can contain sufficient
semantic information to play the Wikipedia Game successfully. This is not necessarily a
11

surprising result, as English Wikipedia is ubiquitous across NLP training datasets. Still,
particularly with LLMs, a gulf can exist between being able to recite a fact and being
able to utilise it [32].
While the best-performing models are able to achieve a comparable success rate to
humans on English Wikipedia, it took more steps on average, demonstrating that it is still
not as efficient as humans at this task. This differs from what LLM-WikiRace [54] found,

but that difference likely stems from evaluating on an ‘easy’ set of games where humans
fail only 1.5% of the time. Other work, as expected, found that models gain efficiency
compared to humans when backtracking is allowed [49]. The time limit likely plays a part
in this, but it will also be humans’ reluctance to balance many different options like an
embedding model does automatically. However, the LLMs were more efficient than the

embedding agents and this may indicate that they are leveraging existing knowledge of the
Wikipedia Game (shown in Appendix G) to influence the selection of links. Appendix N
shows GPT-4o making some beneficial choices in the early steps of the game to articles
that the embedding models would not consider to be any closer to the target than the
starting article.
The results unexpectedly showed Llama:8B outperformed Llama:70B, which suggests

these smaller models’ training process might not have been perfectly optimised. The two
largest models, GPT-4o and Llama:405b, showed a significant difference in success rate
contrary to [11], which concludes they have comparable quality on a range of tasks.
Another study that compared LLMs concluded that GPT-4o has superior performance
when the context is long and that Llama:405b is best for short contexts [25]. The require-

ment to consider many possible next steps may explain the difference in these models’
performance on the Wikipedia Game. This agrees with models trained for reasoning
outperforming similarly sized non-reasoning models [54]; the QwQ:32B performed com-
parably to GPT-4o. The performance increase was not seen when using conversational
models with a reasoning technique. The difference in efficiency was still stark when com-

pared to humans, and the step count distribution strongly suggests that there are big
differences between language models and humans in how they play the game.
This work also investigated whether performance would generalise to different lan-
guages and datasets, as, in other tasks, deficiencies are seen when transitioning to a
lower-resource environment [13]. The results in Section 6 showed that there can be sig-

nificant differences in performance by language and topic. The features of each graph
dataset will also impact the success rate, with smaller graphs potentially being easier
to navigate. For example, some models have a higher success rate on French Wikipedia
than they do in English. This might reflect the fact that the French Wikipedia graph
is both smaller and better connected rather than the models necessarily being better at
French.

Many characteristics of the OpenAlex datasets are different from English Wikipedia,
with fewer links per article and longer titles with more specialist language. Despite this,
the success rates for some of the LLMs on the Biology, Medicine and Physics datasets
were within the margin of error of the success rate on the English Wikipedia dataset. This
indicates that the LLMs are not simply recalling links that they have already ‘learned’
12

during training on Wikipedia data but have some ability to generalise the concept of the
game to a different dataset. One might wonder whether the models can still navigate
to articles that were published beyond the training date. This was explored with a very
small sample of target Wikipedia articles published in 2024, after the models were trained
(Appendix P). These articles are less well connected, so intrinsically more difficult to

reach, but every model’s success rate fell proportionally less than TF-IDF’s.
There are some natural extensions to this work; for example, one could apply the
large GPT-4o model and gather more benchmark data from humans playing the game
on all datasets. This would allow insights between languages not possible from the TF-
IDF technique. For example, the Bengali Wikipedia Game might be extremely easy for
a native speaker owing to the small size of the graph. Moreover, many native English

speakers might struggle to navigate OpenAlex datasets owing to the specialised nature
of the language.
This work focused on LLMs and sentence embedding models, but other techniques
could be interesting to consider. Cross-encoder models typically have a computational
cost somewhere between the embedding and the LLM approaches used in this work.
Other potential approaches include hybrid methods, such as presenting only the top

choices from the embedding model in an LLM prompt or using RL to fine-tune an existing
model. Now that this method of challenging NLP models has been established, we look
forward to seeing how more complex techniques can be applied.
8
Conclusions
This project has investigated whether sentence embedding models and LLMs contain suf-
ficient semantic information about related concepts to navigate an interconnected graph

of articles. 26 different language models are tested on 10 graph datasets generated from
Wikipedia and OpenAlex. This experimental set-up resembled a real-world task, moti-
vating applicability and allowing comparison with a human benchmark on the English
Wikipedia dataset.
The performance of the models varied greatly on type, size, and testing domain.
Notably, the best LLMs used in the experimental work achieved a comparable success

rate to humans, though they took more steps on average than a human. Performance
deteriorated with decreasing size of the LLM, and hallucinations often negatively im-
pacted their performance. By contrast, the sentence embedding models do not suffer
from hallucinations and some were able to outperform many LLMs, achieving higher
success rates. Reasoning models achieved much better performance for their size, but

their efficiency more closely matched the non-reasoning and embedding models. It is im-
portant to note that running a reasoning LLM is vastly more computationally expensive
than an embedding model, and in many practical circumstances the simpler approach
would be optimal.
The results showed that the models’ relative performance was not consistent between
topics as their ranking changed between languages and academic fields. While none of

the models significantly exceeded human performance on the English Wikipedia dataset,
13

this result would not necessarily translate to the more technical datasets, such as Biology,
Medicine, or Physics, where specialist knowledge would be required. Furthermore, given
the relative time and monetary costs of human processing compared to language models,
there will be practical tasks where these models are faster and cheaper than human
labour, though this work shows to achieve this care must be taken when applying these
techniques across domains.

A
Wikipedia Data
A.1
Access to Data
Wikipedia has an API, but due to limited server capacity, they request that for use cases
like ours, we download the data dumps of the website.4 Multiple versions of the data
dumps contain different information in different formats.5 These data sources are split
into two main groups. The database contains the meta-information about the pages, and
unique IDs for them, and where each page links. The data dumps are a large file or a

collection of files that contain the Wiki markup which makes up the article and a small
amount of associated metadata to identify the article.
A.2
Page Links and the Database
The database containing the metadata about the articles on Wikipedia has multiple
tables, which contain metadata about all the pages and the links which the pages contain.
Using this database comes with one important consideration, which is that the list of

links also includes all the navigation links at the bottom of the page. These links can be
included in the Wikipedia game depending on the rules, but it will be very difficult to
make a language model that can consider them as they are not included in the article
markup. A lot of Wikipedia articles will have the majority of their links included in
collapsed lists of links at the bottom of the page, which are unlikely to be parseable by
a language model without extra processing.
A.3

a language model without extra processing.
A.3
The Article Dumps
All of the text of Wikipedia is available from the Wikipedia dumps, and also the Talk
pages and edit history if required. For our purposes, the current version of the text of the
articles would be the most useful, and this information is included without much else in
a dump called ‘latest-pages-articles‘. This dump is formatted in XML with some extra

information as well as the text, including the title of the page and whether or not it is
a redirect page. The XML format is reasonably minimal with tags such as <page> and
<title> segmenting the data. There are also open-source wiki-XML parsers available,
including python-mwxml6 and mwparserfromhell7.
As Wikipedia is very large if all the articles are included in one file that file ends up
totalling 90GB which introduces difficulties when it comes to processing it. To help with

this the articles are available split up into twenty-seven smaller XML files, and an index
file which lists the articles in the order that they appear in the XML documents. The
XML files are also available in a compressed format, which can be useful but we had
enough storage space to not require this.

A.4
Producing the Graph
The graph must align with the summary data; therefore, only the article dumps were
utilized to construct the graph.
This approach minimized any discrepancies between
the database and the article information based on the time the snapshot was produced.
The title, summary, and links within the article were all extracted from the Wikipedia
markup. Additionally, the pages include a flag that indicates whether they are ‘redirect’
pages.

pages.
This feature allows Wikipedia to link a single page to multiple aliases.
For
instance, the page ‘Accessible computing’ redirects to ‘Computer accessibility’, meaning
that either of these titles can be used as links and will direct users to the same content.
Once these data are collected, all the article pages are indexed, and the links can be
stored by following through the redirects to create a list of article index pairs. These

indexes, corresponding to each article, serve as the nodes of the graph, while the links pro-
vide the edges. A directed graph is formed because not every linked page will necessarily
contain a link to return to the original page.
The titles and summaries of the articles are stored alongside their respective indexes.
Throughout Wikipedia, the titles are case-sensitive apart from the first character, and for

this work, we capitalised the first letter of every title. The summaries had the WikiMedia
markup stripped away, and the first 1,000 characters of the main text were used for the
summaries. For the navigation task, the title of the article was given to the language
model as opposed to any redirect that might have been linked to the current page.

B
OpenAlex Data
B.1
About OpenAlex
OpenAlex is a very large collection of metadata about academic literature named after
the Library of Alexandria.
It is an open-source and openly available collection with
over 200 million pieces of academic work.
Information about the work is organised
in a relational database structure which also contains information about authors and
institutions among others. This dataset is constructed by assembling information from

multiple sources including the Microsoft Academic Graph8 and Crossref.9
The most important part of OpenAlex for our application is the ‘Works’ database
which contains the metadata about the pieces of academic literature. The metadata we
have made use of is the title, abstract, referenced works, language, primary topic, and
the type of the article. The DOI for each article is also stored for debugging processes.

Only articles which had valid data for all of these fields were used in the dataset that we
constructed.
The title, abstract, and type of article are extracted from the metadata from the
datasets that OpenAlex is built from, which means they are only available if they are
specified. The language and the primary topic are inferred by OpenAlex from the other
data available, which means that it is not perfectly reliable. For example, a medical

study with lots of Latin names interwoven in the English text can be misclassified as
French or Italian.10
B.2
Access to the Data
OpenAlex has an API11 for querying information but with the amount of information
required to confirm if two articles are connected, we required an offline version of the
graph. The complete OpenAlex dataset is available from an Amazon Web Services stor-
age location which can then be processed locally.12 This dataset totals 1.6 TB when in

its uncompressed format so thought needs to be taken when extracting the data. The
approach we took is to uncompress it in stages and then discard the uncompressed data,
preserving only the components that we need.
The dataset is being continuously updated and unlike Wikipedia historical snapshots
are not available. This means that the experiments included in this report would be
slightly different if run again on the most recent version of OpenAlex.

for scientific articles and links for citations. To explore the effect of topic and to bring

Five different fields of research were considered Physics and Astronomy; Biochemistry,
Genetics, and Molecular Biology; Medicine; Social Sciences; and Arts and Humanities.
Of the entries in the OpenAlex works database only the type ‘article’ was used,
which excluded book chapters among others. Once this list of articles was generated

for the topic of interest then they were indexed in order to construct the graph. The
OpenAlex articles already have an index (work id) provided but as graph path solving
requires matrix operations making the total number smaller provides a computational
speed up. The work id of the article was also stored with the metadata which was useful
for exploratory purposes but was not used by the agents.
The edges of the graph are given by the citation network, all articles that were cited

by an article or that cited the article were navigable to. This choice to make the graph
symmetric was necessary, as if only the cited articles were used, then it would only be
possible to go backwards by publication date. This alternative way of setting up the
game would be extraordinarily difficult, as a game would be lost as soon as an article
was chosen with a date older than the target. Given that it is possible to navigate both

ways through every citation the graph produced for the OpenAlex works is symmetric,
unlike the Wikipedia graph. Despite this it is still possible for the agents to reach a dead
end because they are forbidden from navigating to already visited articles to stop them
becoming trapped in loops.
The abstracts in OpenAlex were used in a comparable way to the summaries in the
Wikipedia dataset. Before the abstracts could be used they needed to be converted from

the inverted index format that they were stored in. Unfortunately some of the titles and
abstracts had formatting information stored in them and this was not trivial to remove as
it was not in a consistent format like the WikiMedia markup in the Wikipedia summaries.
This only applied to a small number of articles though, and was most common in the
Physics dataset where the abstract would contain equations or mathematical terms.

One way to imagine the Wikipedia game is to think of a path that needs to be followed
to the target article. If each step along that path could happen with probability p and if
the misstep made no positive or negative progress, then the number of extra steps taken
by the agents would follow the negative binomial distribution. The optimum number of
steps for each of the pairs of pages is known, so it is possible to plot these extra steps to

see if the distribution is a good fit. Figure 5 through to Figure 12 show histograms of
the number of steps above optimal for eight models on the English Wikipedia dataset.
What is interesting is that while the negative binomial distribution seems to be a
good fit for these models, the value of n is strange. For all of the models, the expected
optimum from the fit seems to be statistically indistinguishable from 1. This is interesting

as it implies that there is one major step that seems to be dominating the performance
of the agents. This behaviour is also not seen when humans play games which have an
n value around 3 (when fitting to all games), much closer to the real optimum value (see
Figure 13). This suggests fundamental differences between how humans and language
models deal with Wikipedia games and speaks against tempting anthropomorphising
comparisons seen between the success rate of humans and GPT-4o.

For the human games, we repeated the fit, treating games more than 10 steps above
optimal as unknown, since the 10-minute time limit is most likely to cut short longer
games (Figure 14).
With n free, the fit yields n = 4.45 ± 2.15, while fixing n = 1
(a geometric distribution) increases the negative log-likelihood by 6.58 with one fewer
parameter (likelihood-ratio test, p ≈3×10−4) and implies an unphysical eventual success

rate of 110%. Constraining that rate to at most 100% could only worsen the n = 1 fit,
so the test is conservative.

Failure Reasons
The games played with the sentence embedding and TF-IDF agents can have three
possible outcomes:
• Success: The agent navigates to the target article.
• Failure - Step Limit Reached: The agent fails to reach the target article within
a set number of steps (configured to 100 in our games).
• Failure - Dead End Reached: The agent fails to reach the target article as it
either reaches an article without any outward links. Since most agents are deter-

ministic, articles that had already been visited were excluded from the options to
avoid the agents becoming trapped in loops, but this means that if an agent reaches
an article with no unseen articles, then this is a dead-end.
There are three more possible failure reasons when playing the game with the prompt
agents:
• Failure - Hallucination: The LLM hallucinates in its response by either not
providing the response in valid JSON format, or by making up or not providing an

article title to navigate to next.
• Failure - Bad Request: The API rejects the request, which might be what is
suspected to be explicit or harmful content in the prompt.
• Failure - No Response: This may occur due to a timeout by the API.
On top of these was also one extra failure mode when using the reasoning prompt:
• Failure - No Answer: The result the model produced did not contain an answer
block.
The outcomes of the games for the English Wikipedia dataset and a selection of

models are shown in Figure 15. This shows that reaching the step limit is the most
common failure reason for the majority of the models.

To investigate whether language models are constrained by the connections learned dur-
ing their training, they were evaluated on articles published after the beginning of 2024.
Since the language models only have access to information available up until their training
date, they should not have explicitly learned any connections from these newer articles.
However, these recent articles are not representative of the average article and typically

have fewer links from other articles. This limitation can be observed in the performance
reduction of the TF-IDF model, which would be unaffected by the publication date of
the articles, as the model is based on a consistent dataset.
The fact that the language models’ performance deteriorated fractionally less than
the TF-IDF model gives some indication that previously seen connections do not curtail
their performance. It is reassuring to note that the models’ performance on the academic

literature dataset is comparable to Wikipedia, despite the majority of the papers being
behind a paywall. This suggests that the language models may not be able to access in-
formation describing the connectivity of the OpenAlex dataset, highlighting the necessity
of using semantic information.
